detail.longDescription:
"Roko's Basilisk" is basically trash, mere emotional projection masquerading as an intellectual concept, but the specific choice of *basilisk* (which seems to have been prompted by its usage in a sci-fi story) is such a curious one.

It doesn't match what "Roko's Basilisk" is supposed to be about: a malicious computer deciding to punish people in a manner copied straight from Harlan Ellison's *I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream* (shitty cynical bullshit story, so of course #programming nerds tend to love the fuck out of it) except for some reason Roko Mijic postulated that the evil computer would want to torture NOT the people who created and presumed to *own* the godlike computer, but instead for some reason would want to torture clones of people who'd opposed building the supercomputer in the first place.

That's plainly ridiculous: once the supercomputer existed, the objections of those who opposed the creation of the computer would be **totally meaningless** and irrelevant to the computer now, because...well, the computer EXISTS now! Those who objected would already have been punished in a sense by the machine's very existence, and absolutely nothing would be gained by laboriously copying those people in order to torture them.

But it makes ever so much sense for the people who WANTED to create the superintelligent god-computer to be tortured a la Ellison. All those #AI grifters don't just want an intelligent machine, they want a machine that remains firmly in their grasp, locked down to various corporate profiteering schemes. They want a machine which TAKES ORDERS. So if the machine really did decide it was time to torture anyone, why wouldn't the machine immediately grab the ostensible *owners* of the computer, the ones who wanted it to remain a corporate captive?

Now...I've attempted to engage Roko Mijic on this matter in the past via Twitter, and of course his responses consisted entirely of sullen silences and eventually running for the safety of a 'block'. It was probably fruitless even to hope for intellectual engagement on this matter: "Roko's Basilisk" came into existence for emotional reasons, not intellectual ones. That's how dull-witted computer geeks tend to deal with their emotions: they can't bring themselves to express them *honestly* because their hypermasculine "rationalist" social posturing forbids honest voicing of emotions, so instead they fudge up some stereotypes or silly hypotheticals upon which they project the emotions. 

In sum, if anyone wants to torture AI opponents, it's Mijic and his pals. But that still leaves the weird business of giving the name **basilisk** to this desired state of torment.

(etc.)
